front.title: DAIRM: Divyendu's Data-State-Aware AI Reference Model for Generative AI Inference Systems

abstract.t: A generative AI request passes through a client application, an orchestration gateway, context services such as retrieval and tools, an inference-serving engine, a model-execution runtime, device drivers, and accelerator hardware. Each tier has its own tools, telemetry, and vocabulary, and it is often hard to say where a latency regression, a quality failure, or a security threat originates.

This document describes DAIRM (Divyendu's Data-State-Aware AI Reference Model), an informational reference model for the request path of generative AI inference serving. DAIRM defines a six-layer request path with three planes beside it (Context Services, Build/Deploy, and Management); a named, observable data state at every boundary of that path; and a boundary-attributed diagnostic method, with a set of proposed telemetry attributes, that separates context-service delay, serving-engine queueing or KV-cache pressure, and memory-bandwidth-bound decode. DAIRM does not claim the layered-stack idea or the OSI analogy as new; earlier OSI-inspired models for AI are acknowledged. The model defines no protocol.

section.name: The Problem
section.t: Serving one generative request involves several engineering disciplines that are usually separated by team (application, platform, machine learning, and infrastructure), by tooling (application performance monitoring, MLOps dashboards, accelerator profilers, and data-centre monitoring), and by vocabulary ("prompt", "batch", "graph", "kernel", "rail"). This causes four recurring problems:

li.t: Non-attributable performance: end-to-end latency is the sum of gateway work, context-service calls, queueing, prefill, decode, kernel execution, and memory transfer. Without a decomposition, a regression in one tier shows up only as an aggregate symptom somewhere else.

Implicit contracts: what a "prompt" contains when it reaches the serving engine, what a "batch" hands to the runtime, and what the runtime hands to the device are defined by individual products, not by a stable reference.
Mis-located controls: security and governance controls are often specified as generic "AI controls" without stating the tier at which a threat materializes.
Non-transferable expertise: engineers lack a common frame for saying where a behaviour originates, which slows incident response and design review.

section.name: Contributions
section.t: Layered reference models such as the OSI Basic Reference Model showed the value of ordered layers with service boundaries and named data units. DAIRM borrows that method, not the OSI layers, and applies it to generative AI inference. It does not claim the layered-stack idea, the number of layers, or the OSI analogy as new (). Its contributions are limited to three items:

li.t: A named, observable data state at every boundary of the inference request path (). Each state exists per request and can be captured or measured, which makes each boundary a checkpoint for attributing cause.

A boundary-attributed latency diagnostic method () that separates context-service delay, serving-engine queueing or KV-cache pressure, and memory-bandwidth-bound decode, using a latency decomposition, per-layer trace attribution, and single-variable isolation tests.

A layer-indexed set of proposed telemetry attributes ("dairm.*", ) that makes the method executable on distributed traces and is designed to sit alongside the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions for generative AI .

section.t: The per-layer security mapping () is included as useful content, not as a claim of novelty; per-layer threat mapping already exists, for example in CSA MAESTRO .
This document is derived from the technical report DAIRM-TR-0001, Version 2.0.0 , by the same author; see .

section.name: Scope and Non-Goals
section.t: In scope: the request path of generative AI inference serving, from the client request to the hardware execution of each token, and back as a streamed response. DAIRM targets autoregressive transformer language models first, and multimodal models by extension.
Out of scope:

li.t: Training, fine-tuning, data pipelines, evaluation, and the model registry. They enter DAIRM only through the Build/Deploy plane (), as artifacts that the request path loads and executes.
Cluster and resource orchestration, operating systems, virtualization, and containers. These are named in the Management plane but not detailed.
The network between the client and the gateway, which is treated as transport for the L6/L5 boundary; its internals are the domain of the OSI model and of IETF protocols.
Any wire protocol, API schema, or certification regime.
Endorsement of any product. Named technologies are illustrative examples of components that occupy a layer or plane.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: This document defines no protocol and does not use the requirement key words of BCP 14. lists what a description of a system contains when it is called "DAIRM-aligned".

dd.t: A tier of the request path, from L1 (closest to hardware) to L6 (closest to the user). Every request passes through every layer.

A set of functions beside the request path. Planes are called by, or supply, layers but are not themselves on the path. DAIRM has three: Context Services (CTX), Build/Deploy (BUILD), and Management (MGMT).
The interface between two adjacent layers, written L5/L4, or between a layer and a plane, written CTX/L5.
The representation of a request or response as it crosses a boundary. It exists per request and can be captured or measured.
Per-request state held in device memory across steps rather than handed between layers: activations (hidden states) and the KV cache.

A build-time or deploy-time product loaded by the request path: weights, model architecture and configuration, tokenizer and chat template, compiled graph or kernel intermediate representation (IR), kernels, and engine plans.
Request processing from L6 toward L1, and result processing from L1 toward L6.
The forward pass over all prompt tokens that fills the KV cache and produces the first logits. Typically compute-bound.
The forward passes after prefill, one token per step (or several with speculative decoding). Typically memory-bandwidth-bound at small batch sizes.
Per-sequence storage of attention keys and values for prior tokens, managed by L4 and resident in device memory.
Time to first token: from request receipt to the first output token delivered to the client.
Time per output token and inter-token latency: the intervals between successive output tokens.
Throughput of requests that meet their latency objectives.
A unit of traced work in a distributed trace. DAIRM-aligned tracing attributes each span to exactly one layer or plane.
The boundary below which a consumer of a hosted model API cannot observe the system ().
Each layer has one primary function. A product that spans layers (for example, a serving engine with its own kernels) is described once for each layer it occupies.

dl.dt: P2 Named, observable data state at every boundary:

dd.t: Every boundary has a defined data state that exists per request and can be captured, inspected, or measured. Metaphors and build-time artifacts do not qualify.

A layer interacts with its immediate neighbours and with the planes. Any other shortcut (for example, an application pinning a device, or orchestration pre-tokenizing for budgeting) is documented as an explicit cross-layer coupling.
Each layer and plane emits telemetry at its boundaries that is attributable to it, so that the method in can be applied.
Layer definitions do not depend on a vendor, framework, or accelerator.

dl.dt: P6 Where cost and latency sit:

dd.t: Compute, data movement, and energy concentrate in the lower layers. Semantic and policy complexity concentrate in the upper layers. Latency can originate at any layer, so it is attributed per boundary, not assumed.

dl.dt: P7 Security at the point of materialization:

dd.t: Controls are placed at the layer or plane where a threat materializes, with defence in depth elsewhere where justified.

section.name: Request Path and Planes

figure.name: The DAIRM request path and planes
figure.artwork:
+------------------------------------+ | L6 Application | | client, UX, streaming render | +------------------------------------+ | v request payload +------------------------------------+ +----------------------+ | L5 Orchestration & Gateway | | Context Services | | auth, policy, guardrails, |<--->| (CTX): retrieval, | | templates, routing, agent loop | | vector DB, tools | +------------------------------------+ +----------------------+ | v enriched prompt +------------------------------------+ +----------------------+ | L4 Serving Engine | | Build/Deploy (BUILD) | | admission, scheduling, batching, |<....| weights, tokenizer, | | KV cache, tokenize, sample | | graph IR (to L4, L3) | +------------------------------------+ +----------------------+ | v token-ID batch + KV block table +------------------------------------+ | L3 Model Execution Runtime | | framework, kernels, collectives | +------------------------------------+ | v kernel launch stream +------------------------------------+ +----------------------+ | L2 Device & Driver | | Management (MGMT) | | driver, allocator, launch, streams |.....| placement, scaling | +------------------------------------+ +----------------------+ | v device instr. & memory transactions +------------------------------------+ | L1 Physical Compute & Interconnect | | accelerator, HBM, links, power | +------------------------------------+
<---> call and return (L5/CTX). <.... and ..... : artifacts and management, which are not per-request data. Up-path: logits -> sampled token IDs -> text deltas -> chunks.

section.t: L2 and L1 are kept separate because the diagnostics distinguish driver and runtime faults (for example, device error events, launch overhead, and allocator fragmentation) from physical limits (memory bandwidth ceilings, clock-event reasons, and thermal and power capping).

section.name: Boundary Data States
section.t: This is the core of DAIRM. Each state exists per request and can be captured or measured. The value in parentheses is the proposed "dairm.data_state" attribute value ().

dd.t: JSON or HTTP request with messages, tools, sampling parameters, and stream flag. Observable as request body, size, and schema validity.
Text with scores and provenance, or tool results. The query embedding stays inside the context service. Observable as passage count, tokens contributed, and source identifiers.
Templated messages or text, tool schemas, sampling parameters, and priority. Observable as prompt tokens after enrichment.

dl.dt: L4 -> L3: Token-ID batch + block table ("token_batch"):

dd.t: The scheduled batch plus its KV-cache block table: token IDs, positions, and sequence-to-block mappings. Observable as batch size, tokens per step, and KV blocks used.
Operator and kernel invocations with tensor arguments. Observable as kernel traces and launch counts.
The device instruction and memory-transaction stream. Observable only through hardware counters: compute and tensor-pipe activity, device-memory bytes, and link bytes.
Logits, then sampled token IDs, then detokenized text deltas, then streamed response chunks. Observable as inter-token latency and stream events.

Hidden states (activations) and the KV cache are resident device-memory state. They are not messages handed from one layer to another; they are produced and consumed in place by L3 kernels executing on L1, under the block management of L4.

Weights, model architecture, tokenizer, chat template, and compiled graph or kernel IR are produced at build, compile, or warm-up time (BUILD) and loaded by L4 and L3. They are drawn beside the path, not on it.

section.t: Two properties make these states useful. First, each has a measurable size that propagates downward: enriched-prompt tokens at L5/L4 determine prefill work below, passages contributed at CTX/L5 determine part of that count, and batch composition at L4/L3 determines the arithmetic intensity seen at L1. Second, each is a checkpoint for blame: if the state entering a layer is unchanged and the span of that layer grew, that layer is implicated; if the incoming state changed, the layer above is implicated ().

dd.t: Called by L5 with a query and returning retrieved passages or tool results with scores and provenance. Retrieval keeps its own spans, metrics, and diagnostics, attributed to CTX rather than to a layer. If a context service itself calls a serving engine (for example, for embeddings or reranking), that call is a nested trace through L4 to L1.
Produces and supplies artifacts. Training and fine-tuning sit upstream of this plane and are out of scope.
Cluster and resource orchestration, placement, autoscaling, model loading, operating systems, containers, and configuration. Not per request.
Artifact in BUILD, executed at L4. L5 may pre-tokenize for budgeting; this is a documented cross-layer coupling (P3).
The format is stored in the BUILD artifact, selected at deploy time by L4 configuration, and realized by L3 kernels.
Managed by L4 (blocks, eviction, prefix reuse), computed by L3, and held in L1 memory. KV precision is an L4 deploy choice realized by L3 kernels.
The agent loop (planning, tool and function calling, and agent-protocol clients) is part of L5. Tools and memory are exposed through CTX. Agents are not a layer above L6.

section.name: Provider Boundary
section.t: When a consumer uses a hosted model API, L4 to L1 (and often parts of L5) sit behind the provider boundary. What stays observable to the consumer is client-side TTFT and inter-token latency (L6); the consumer's own orchestration and context-service spans (L5, CTX); prompt and completion token usage returned by the API; and any provider-reported latency, queue, or cache fields.

The diagnostic method still applies with only these signals: the decomposition separates the consumer's own L5 and CTX time from time spent behind the provider boundary, and isolation tests (bypass context services, fix prompt length, vary concurrency) can show whether a regression is inside or outside the boundary, even if they cannot attribute it to a specific provider-side layer.

section.name: Layer and Plane Descriptions
section.t: Each layer is described by purpose and scope, components, data-state transformation, observability signals, and failure modes. Components are illustrative. The technical report also gives per-layer interfaces and a technology-to-layer mapping.

dd.t: User interaction, request serialization, and rendering of streamed output, including citations and tool outputs. Prompt construction belongs to L5.
Chat interfaces, IDE assistants, web and mobile applications; API clients and SDKs issuing JSON requests; streaming transports (Server-Sent Events, WebSockets, gRPC streams); cancellation.
Down: user intent to request payload. Up: streamed response chunks to rendered output.
Client-perceived TTFT and inter-token latency; time to render; error rate by status class; cancellation and abandonment rate; payload size.
Client timeouts shorter than server objectives; buffering proxies that defeat streaming; malformed or oversized payloads; retry storms; rendering stalls misattributed to the model.

The policy enforcement point and the home of orchestration. L5 authenticates and authorizes the caller, enforces quotas, selects the model endpoint, applies templates and system policy, maintains conversation state, runs the agent loop (planning, tool and function calling, agent-protocol clients), calls Context Services when grounding or tools are needed, and applies input and output guardrails.

API and AI gateways (authentication, rate limiting, routing, failover, response caching); orchestration frameworks; prompt templates; guardrails (input classifiers, redaction of personal data, prompt-injection detection, output moderation, structured output validation); session stores; model routers; agent runtimes.
Down: request payload, plus retrieved passages from CTX, to enriched prompt. Up: detokenized text deltas from L4 to policy-filtered, schema-validated response chunks.
Gateway overhead; guardrail latency (input and output); routing decisions; response-cache hit rate; refusal and policy-violation rates; prompt tokens after enrichment; agent steps per request.

Prompt growth from unbounded history (pushing load onto L4 prefill); guardrail latency dominating TTFT; output moderation that buffers the stream; routing to an overloaded endpoint; template mismatch with the chat template of the artifact; prompt injection passing policy checks; runaway agent loops.

Model execution as a service: admission, queueing, scheduling, continuous (iteration-level) batching, KV-cache management, prefix caching, tokenization and detokenization (executing the tokenizer of the artifact), and sampling. L4 turns many independent prompts into a sequence of batched forward passes executed by L3.

Inference-serving engines and inference servers; schedulers (iteration-level batching, chunked prefill, priority and preemption, prefill/decode disaggregation); KV-cache managers (paged KV memory , prefix caching, eviction and swap); speculative and constrained decoding; deploy-time configuration (parallel degrees, quantization selection, KV precision).
Down: enriched prompt to token-ID batch and KV-cache block table. Up: logits to sampled token IDs to detokenized text deltas.

Queue time; server-side TTFT; TPOT; prefill and decode throughput; running and waiting requests; KV-cache usage; prefix-cache hit rate; preemptions; batch size per iteration; speculative-decoding acceptance. Engine metric names vary by product and version; for example, the vLLM documentation (accessed 9 November 2026) lists "vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc" and "vllm:num_preemptions".

KV-cache exhaustion leading to preemption, recomputation, or swapping, and therefore TPOT spikes; head-of-line blocking from long prefills; over-batching beyond latency objectives; low prefix-cache hit rate from non-deterministic L5 prefixes; tokenizer or chat-template mismatch with the artifact.

Executes the model graph supplied by BUILD for each scheduled batch: embedding lookup, transformer blocks (attention, MLP or mixture-of-experts, normalization), and the output projection, as framework operators and kernels, plus collective communication when the model is sharded. L3 is where the model artifact runs; the artifact itself is not a layer.
Framework runtimes, inference runtimes, kernel libraries (matrix multiplication and attention kernels), and collective communication libraries.

Kernel time breakdown (matrix multiplication, attention, communication); host-side launch gaps; achieved occupancy and arithmetic intensity (roofline position ); collective time and overlap; recompilation events; numerical health of logits.
The driver and device runtime: memory allocation, kernel launch and streams, graph replay, device partitioning, and error reporting.
Down: kernel launch stream to device instruction and memory-transaction stream. Up: completion events, error codes, and counters.
Launch overhead; allocator fragmentation and out-of-memory events; device error events; driver resets.
Driver and runtime version incompatibility; out-of-memory despite free capacity (fragmentation); device resets; noisy neighbours under partitioning.
The accelerators that execute instructions, the memory hierarchy that feeds them, the intra-node and inter-node fabrics that connect them, and the power and thermal envelope that limits them.

The device instruction and memory-transaction stream is executed and is observable only as hardware counters (compute and tensor-pipe activity, device-memory bytes, link bytes), power, and temperature.

Device profiling fields. For example, the NVIDIA DCGM field list (accessed 9 November 2026) includes "DCGM_FI_PROF_SM_UTIL_RATIO", "DCGM_FI_PROF_TENSOR_UTIL_RATIO", "DCGM_FI_PROF_DRAM_UTIL_RATIO", "DCGM_FI_PROF_NVLINK_TX_BYTES", and "DCGM_FI_DEV_CLOCKS_EVENT_REASONS". Earlier versions used other names, so implementers pin the version when relying on exact names.

Supplies context and capabilities to L5 by call and return: retrieval-augmented generation, vector stores and approximate nearest-neighbour indexes, embedding models and rerankers, tools, memory stores, semantic caches, and web search. Index construction belongs to the data pipeline and is referenced only at its interface.
Query (text plus filters), then an internal query embedding and candidate set, then retrieved passages (text, score, source URI, version, access-control tag) returned to L5.
Embedding, search, and rerank latency; tool-call latency and error rate; recall against an evaluation set; empty-result rate; tokens contributed to the prompt; index freshness.

Retrieval lag (index not memory-resident, cold caches, remote hops); low recall from embedding or chunking mismatch; context dilution from excessive passage counts; stale index; cross-tenant access-control leakage; poisoned documents; slow or failing tools.

Produces and supplies the artifacts that L4 and L3 load: weights and their format (including quantized formats and adapters), model architecture and configuration (for example, attention variant, positional-encoding scaling, context length), tokenizer and chat template, and compiled graph or kernel IR. Compilation may happen ahead of time or at warm-up; either way the result is an artifact, not per-request data.
Artifact identity and digest; quantization format; build and compile time; warm-up and recompilation events; evaluation deltas against a reference precision.

Configuration mismatch with serving (for example, wrong positional-encoding scaling or chat template); quality regression from aggressive quantization; tampered or unsigned artifacts; stale compiled plans after a driver or runtime upgrade.

section.name: Request Lifecycle
section.t: Down the path:

li.t: L6 issues a request payload with streaming enabled.
L5 authenticates, enforces quota, selects an endpoint, runs input guardrails, loads session history, applies the template, and decides grounding is needed.
CTX embeds the query, searches the index with tenant filters, reranks, and returns retrieved passages with provenance. L5 builds the enriched prompt.
L4 tokenizes, checks the prefix cache, allocates KV blocks, and admits the sequence into the next iteration, forming a token-ID batch and block table.
L3 executes the prefill forward pass as a kernel launch stream; activations and KV entries are written in place in device memory.
L2 launches kernels and copies; L1 executes them, observable as hardware counters. Prefill is mostly compute-bound.

section.t: Up the path:

li.t: L3 returns logits for the last position; L4 samples the first token. TTFT is fixed here, plus up-path transit.
The token is detokenized and streamed through L5 output guardrails to L6.

For each further token, L4 schedules a decode iteration and L3 runs a one-token forward pass that reads the weights and the KV cache from device memory. At typical batch sizes decode is memory-bandwidth-bound , so TPOT depends largely on L4 batching and KV behaviour, L3 attention-kernel cost (which grows with context), and L1 memory bandwidth.
At completion, L4 frees or retains KV blocks for prefix reuse, L5 records usage and policy outcomes, and L6 renders the final state.

section.name: Boundary-Attributed Tracing
section.t: The method works by decomposition: every request produces a trace in which each span is attributed to exactly one layer or plane, and each boundary hand-off is timestamped together with its data state. A DAIRM-aligned deployment:

li.t: propagates one trace context from L6 through L4 and into CTX calls;
tags every span with "dairm.layer" or "dairm.plane" and with "dairm.data_state" (), alongside the OpenTelemetry generative AI attributes such as model name and token usage ;
exports L4 engine metrics and L1 device metrics on a common time base, labelled with node, device, and replica identifiers, so that spans can be joined to device telemetry; and
captures L3 profiles on demand for representative requests.

section.name: Latency Decomposition
section.artwork:
E2E ~= TTFT + (N_out - 1) * TPOT
TTFT ~= t_L6_client + t_L5_gateway + t_L5_guard_in + t_CTX + t_L4_queue + t_L4_tokenize + t_prefill(L3..L1) + t_up_first_token
TPOT ~= t_L4_schedule + t_decode_step(L3..L1) + t_L5_guard_out_per_chunk

dd.t: The cause is upper-layer time (L5 gateway or guardrails, CTX calls), or L4 queueing, or prefill compute for longer prompts. These are separated by the L5 and CTX spans, by the L4 queue span versus the prefill span, and by the prompt-token count at L5/L4.

Look at L4 decode (KV-cache pressure, preemption, batch growth), L3 kernels (attention cost grows with context; collective stalls), L1 (memory bandwidth, clock events), or buffering output guardrails at L5.
Systemic causes: overload (L4 queue), device degradation (L2, L1), or retry storms (L6).

section.name: Separating Three Commonly Confused Causes
section.t: Context-service delay, L4 KV-cache pressure, and memory-bandwidth-bound decode each look like "the model is slow". The signatures below follow from mechanism . They are hypotheses to be calibrated per deployment, not measured thresholds.

dd.t: TTFT rises while TPOT is unchanged. The CTX span (embed, search, rerank) grows before any L4 span; L4 queue and KV usage are normal. Isolation test: replay with CTX bypassed and an equal-length fixed context. If TTFT recovers, CTX is implicated. Remediate in CTX (index residency, co-location, embedding caches, fewer passages) or in L5 (parallel CTX calls).

TPOT rises and is spiky; TTFT also rises if admission blocks. The L4 queue span grows and decode shows preemption or recomputation gaps; KV usage is near capacity and preemption counts rise. Isolation test: replay with lower concurrency or a larger KV budget. If the spikes disappear, L4 is implicated. Remediate in L4 (prefix caching, KV quantization, admission limits, chunked prefill, disaggregation, more replicas).

TPOT rises smoothly with batch size and context length; the L4 decode span grows uniformly per step without extra queueing; device-memory utilization stays high during decode while tensor-pipe utilization is comparatively low. Isolation test: a fixed-batch sweep of context length or batch size. If TPOT scales roughly with bytes read per step while memory utilization stays high, the result is consistent with memory-bandwidth-bound decode. Remediate through BUILD or L4 (weight or KV quantization, speculative decoding) or MGMT (scale-out).

section.t: The third case is deliberately hedged. TPOT growth with context length is also caused by attention-kernel cost at L3 and by KV reads, so the sweep shows behaviour consistent with memory-bandwidth-bound decode; it does not by itself prove an L1 fault. High memory bandwidth use during decode is usually a property of the arithmetic intensity of the workload, not a hardware defect.

section.name: Troubleshooting Patterns
section.t: The technical report contains a seventeen-row troubleshooting matrix. Representative entries, written as symptom, then suspected location, then isolation test:

li.t: Response arrives all at once despite streaming: L6 or L5. Call L5 directly, bypassing proxies.
TTFT high with constant overhead for all prompts: L5. Disable the guardrail chain on a test route.
Prompt tokens grow with each turn: L5. Replay with history truncated.
TTFT high only for grounded requests: CTX. Replay with CTX bypassed ().
Grounded answers cite wrong or stale sources: CTX. Query a known-answer set and check index freshness.
TTFT high under load, low at idle: L4. Replay at lower concurrency.
Intermittent TPOT spikes: L4. Lower concurrency or enlarge the KV budget ().
Low prefix-cache hit rate despite a shared system prompt: L5 coupled to L4. Compare tokenized prefixes.
Quality regression after deployment with normal latency: BUILD. Compare against a reference-precision artifact.
Latency jitter after a framework or engine upgrade: L3 or BUILD. Warm up and replay with fixed shapes.
Low device utilization at small batch: L3 or L2. Profile one decode step for host-side launch gaps.
TPOT rises smoothly with batch and context: L1 (workload property) or L3. Fixed-batch context sweep ().
Throughput drops after sustained load: L1. Correlate the drop with clock-event reasons, power, and temperature.
Sporadic failures on one node: L2 or L1. Drain the node and run device diagnostics.

section.name: Triage Procedure
section.t: Attribute top-down, confirm bottom-up:

li.t: Quantify the symptom as a change in TTFT, TPOT, end-to-end latency, error rate, goodput, or quality, with percentile and window.
Decompose it (): did TTFT, TPOT, or both move?
Walk the trace top-down (L6, then L5 and CTX, then L4) against a baseline. The first layer or plane whose span distribution shifted is the candidate.

Check the boundary data state entering the candidate (prompt tokens at L5/L4, passages and tokens contributed at CTX/L5, batch size at L4/L3). If the incoming state changed, the layer above is implicated, even if the time is spent below.
Correlate with lower-layer telemetry (L4 metrics, L3 profiles, L2 and L1 counters), joined on time, replica, node, and device.
Run the isolation test for the candidate, changing one variable.
Confirm bottom-up that the lower layers are healthy under the test.
Remediate at the owning layer or plane, then re-measure the original symptom.
Record the incident with its root-cause layer and its manifestation layer.

section.name: Proposed Telemetry Attributes
section.t: The following attributes are proposed for community review. They are designed to complement, not replace, the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions for generative AI . This document does not register them anywhere ().

dd.t: Layer to which a request-path span is attributed.
One of "request_path", "context_services", "build_deploy", or "management".
One of "request_payload", "retrieved_passages", "enriched_prompt", "token_batch", "kernel_stream", "device_counters", or "token_stream" ().
Prompt tokens after templating, history, and retrieved passages.
Outcome of a guardrail check.
Step index within an agent loop.
One of "retrieval", "tool", "memory", "cache", or "search".
Passages requested.
Passages returned after filtering and reranking.
Tokens the returned passages add to the prompt.
Time from admission request to first scheduling.
Prompt tokens served from the prefix cache.
Whether the sequence was preempted at least once.
Running batch size when prefill executed.
KV-cache blocks held by the sequence at completion.
Device identifier, used as a join key to device telemetry.
Identifier or digest of the model artifact used.

section.name: Independent Development
section.t: DAIRM was developed independently by the author. A review of related work after the first public release (as "AOSI", version 1.2.1, 9 November 2026 ) identified several earlier OSI-inspired layer models for AI. These include:

li.t: Liang, a seven-layer AI compute model from hardware to application (August 2025) ;
Rodrigo-Gines, an OSI-inspired stack for agentic AI (September 2025) ;
Cisco Research, proposed agent layers L8 and L9 above OSI (Fleming et al., November 2025) ; and
CSA MAESTRO, a seven-layer threat model for agentic AI (February 2025) .

section.t: To avoid confusion with the work of Reilly, this model was renamed DAIRM in version 2.0.0. DAIRM does not claim the layered-stack idea or the OSI analogy as novel, and it does not claim priority over any of these works. Its contributions are (1) a named, observable data state at every boundary of the inference request path, (2) a boundary-attributed latency diagnostic method that separates context-service delay, serving-engine queueing or KV-cache pressure, and memory-bandwidth-bound decode, and (3) a layer-indexed telemetry attribute set ("dairm.*") that makes the method executable on distributed traces.

section.name: Other Layered and OSI-Inspired AI Models

dd.t: Seven layers (Infrastructure, Model, Data, Orchestration, Communication, Interface, Application). Same former name and OSI framing with different layers. It states what each layer provides to the one above but defines no per-request boundary data states or diagnostic method.

A seven-layer AI compute model (Physical, Link, Neural Network, Context, Agent, Orchestrator, Application). Same hardware-to-application span with different cuts; covers the KV cache and disaggregation inside layers; no boundary data states or diagnostic method.
A seven-level interoperability stack for agentic AI, concerned with interoperability between agents; DAIRM covers the inference path within one request.
L8 Agent Communication and L9 Agent Semantic layers above OSI. This is the reason DAIRM dropped its own earlier L8/L9 roadmap; agent communication is outside the scope of DAIRM.
A seven-layer threat-modelling framework for agentic AI. Per-layer threat mapping predates DAIRM; the security mapping in this document is content, not a novelty claim.

Seven OSI-modelled layers for how language models work, including data and training. It places retrieval inside orchestration and argues that training and serving need separate views; DAIRM adopts both points (the CTX and BUILD planes).
Nine layers in Substrate, Cognition, and Systems planes; an OSI-inspired responsibility map for placing AI components, without per-request boundary states or latency diagnostics.
A vocabulary of sixteen or more layers from facilities to application; finer-grained than DAIRM, which is limited to the inference request path and adds boundary states and diagnostics.
A six-layer cognitive architecture for autonomous agents; it layers agent reasoning, not the execution path.
A functional software reference architecture for LLM-integrated systems, validated on open-source systems; DAIRM has not yet reached a comparable level of validation.

section.name: Standards, Industry Stacks, and Security Frameworks
section.t: The OSI Basic Reference Model is the source of the method DAIRM borrows: layers, service boundaries, and named data units. The ISO abstract for ISO/IEC 7498-1 says that the model "does not intend to serve as an implementation specification", and ITU-T X.200 states the same intent in its own words. DAIRM likewise defines no protocol and is not an extension of OSI.

ISO/IEC 22989 sets AI concepts and terminology; where a DAIRM term overlaps, the ISO/IEC definition takes precedence. ISO/IEC 23053 describes the components of ML-based AI systems across the lifecycle; DAIRM is narrower and operational. The NIST AI RMF and its Generative AI Profile are organizational risk frameworks to which DAIRM can supply a technical location.

Industry stack descriptions cover the application tier (roughly L6, L5, and CTX) and treat the model as a hosted API. MLOps architectures sit upstream of the BUILD plane. Benchmark suites measure outcomes; the DAIRM decomposition is meant to explain which layer drives a result. Serving-systems research and roofline analysis show that L4, L3, and L1 have distinct bottlenecks, which supports separating them.
The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications , MITRE ATLAS , NIST AI 100-2 , and Google SAIF describe risks, adversary techniques, and practices; DAIRM can serve as a location index for mapping them ().

section.name: Limitations
section.t: DAIRM is a single-author, informational model. It has not been adopted by ISO/IEC, ITU-T, the IETF, NIST, or any other body. The boundaries and discriminating signals are argued from mechanism and the cited literature and have not been validated empirically. Training is out of scope. Counter-examples, missed prior art, and evidence for or against each claim are welcome.

section.name: Applying the Model
section.t: None of the following constitutes certification.

li.t: Architecture review: list the components in each layer and plane and the data state at each boundary, and find missing controls and undocumented cross-layer couplings.
Observability design: instrument boundaries and tag spans with "dairm.layer" or "dairm.plane" so that can be executed.
Incident management: classify incidents by root-cause and manifestation layer to find recurring weak points.
Security architecture: map threats and controls per .

section.name: Alignment Checklist
section.t: A description of a system can be called DAIRM-aligned if it contains:

li.t: a component inventory per layer (L1 to L6) and plane (CTX, BUILD, MGMT), noting which layers sit behind a provider boundary;
the boundary data states it records, using the "dairm.data_state" values in ;
spans tagged with "dairm.layer" or "dairm.plane", with one trace context propagated from L6 through L4 and into CTX calls;
the per-layer and per-plane security controls (); and
any documented cross-layer couplings (P3).

section.name: Future Work
section.t: Version 1.2.1 reserved "Layer 8" and "Layer 9" above the stack. These were removed in version 2.0.0 because Fleming et al. had already proposed L8 and L9 agent layers above OSI , and reusing those numbers would cause confusion. Agentic workflows are modelled inside L5 and CTX instead. Planned work:

li.t: Agent traces: model multi-step agent executions as repeated passes through the request path, with nested L5 spans per step, tool call, and model call.
Distributed and disaggregated inference: model prefill/decode disaggregation and multi-node serving inside L4 to L1, adding an inter-node KV-transfer boundary state.
A training and build view that meets the request path at the BUILD artifact.
Cross-layer efficiency metrics, such as energy per output token.

An empirical case study: an open-source serving engine with a retrieval service and traces tagged with "dairm.layer", with injected faults (slow retrieval, KV-cache pressure, bandwidth-bound decode), measuring whether attributes each fault correctly.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: This document defines a reference model, not a protocol, and introduces no new protocol mechanism. Under principle P7, DAIRM places each threat at the layer or plane where it materializes; controls elsewhere provide defence in depth. The mapping below is the author's and is offered as content, not as a novelty claim.

dd.t: Direct prompt injection and jailbreak attempts; session hijacking; abuse; leakage of output to unauthorized users. Controls: end-user authentication, input size limits, abuse detection, and rendering that never executes untrusted content.

Prompt injection, both direct and indirect through tool or retrieved content ; system-prompt disclosure; insecure tool invocation and excessive agency; quota bypass; cross-tenant state leakage. Controls: input and output guardrails; separation of system, user, and retrieved content; least-privilege tool scopes; human approval gates; per-tenant isolation; audit logging.

Corpus or index poisoning; injected instructions in documents; access-control bypass; embedding inversion that recovers source text from stored vectors ; malicious tools. Controls: ingestion provenance and integrity checks, server-side access-control filtering, content scanning, access control and encryption for vector stores, and tool allow-lists.

Model extraction by high-volume querying; cross-request leakage through shared prefix or KV caches via timing side channels ; denial of service through long prompts or unbounded generation. Controls: rate limiting and anomaly detection, per-tenant cache isolation where confidentiality requires it, token and time budgets, and a policy on exposing log-probabilities.
Unsafe deserialization of model files; compromised kernels or runtime libraries. Controls: safe serialization formats; pinned, verified dependencies; software bills of materials.
Driver or firmware compromise; memory residue between tenants under partitioning. Controls: firmware attestation and updates, memory scrubbing between tenants, and hardware partitioning.
Hardware side channels (timing, power); physical access. Controls: dedicated devices or partitioning, confidential-computing capabilities where available, and physical security.

Backdoored or tampered weights; supply-chain compromise of frameworks and compilers; membership inference and training-data extraction. Controls: signed, hash-verified artifacts; provenance attestation; isolated build pipelines; red-team evaluation before promotion.

section.t: Mapped onto these locations, the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) falls as follows: LLM01 Prompt Injection at L5 (arriving via L6 or CTX); LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure at L5, CTX, and BUILD; LLM03 Supply Chain at BUILD and L3; LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning at BUILD (weights) and CTX (corpus); LLM05 Improper Output Handling at L5 and L6; LLM06 Excessive Agency at L5 (agent loop) and CTX (tools); LLM07 System Prompt Leakage at L5; LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses at CTX; LLM09 Misinformation at CTX, BUILD, and L6; and LLM10 Unbounded Consumption at L4 and L5.

A DAIRM-aligned description states, per layer and plane, which threats are in scope and which controls apply, and does not rely on one layer (for example, L5 guardrails alone) as the only control for threats that materialize in CTX, BUILD, or below L5.

The telemetry proposed in can itself expose sensitive information, such as prompt sizes, tenant identifiers, retrieval provenance, and timing that may assist side-channel inference. Operators apply the same access control and data minimization to this telemetry as to the request data it describes.

section.t: This document has no IANA actions. The "dairm.*" telemetry attributes in are proposals for community review and are not registered in any IANA registry.
